analysis.one_liner: Caps punitive damages in financial-injury lawsuits at three times actual losses or $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in October 1998 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which took no action before Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so it never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would apply nationwide to civil lawsuits in federal and state court that affect interstate commerce, mainly cases where a plaintiff sues a company over money losses like fraud or bad insurance practices. It would raise the bar for winning punitive damages — the extra money a jury can add to punish misconduct — requiring clear and convincing proof that the defendant acted with flagrant indifference to others' rights or safety. It would also cap punitive awards at the greater of three times the actual financial loss or $250,000, with an even lower cap for individuals and businesses with fewer than 25 employees. Cases involving death, serious physical injury, drunk driving, or convicted violent crimes would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies, insurers, and other defendants facing lawsuits over financial misconduct. They would face a higher burden of proof for punitive damages and a firm ceiling on how much a jury could award, limiting the largest and most unpredictable verdicts and reducing the cost of defending and settling such cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses and insurers facing damage suits

how_it_helps.text: Punitive damages could be awarded only if the claimant proves by clear and convincing evidence — a stricter standard than ordinary civil proof — that the defendant acted with conscious, flagrant indifference to the rights or safety of others [S2].

Punitive awards would be capped at the greater of three times the economic loss or $250,000, and at the lesser of those two amounts against individuals with a net worth under $500,000 and organizations with fewer than 25 full-time employees [S2].

The bill's findings argue that large punitive verdicts raise consumer prices and cause products and services to be withdrawn from the market, citing a Rand study showing average punitive verdicts in financial-injury cases rose from $3.4 million to $7.6 million between the late 1980s and early 1990s [S3].
The jury would not be told about the caps, and any party could force a separate proceeding on punitive damages, with punitive-only evidence kept out of the compensatory-damages phase [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and investors who sue over financial wrongdoing — for example, insurance bad faith, investment fraud, or deceptive billing. Their potential punishment awards would be capped, harder to win, and decided without the jury hearing the full story of the misconduct in the first phase of trial. State courts would have to apply the federal rules even where state law is more generous to injured plaintiffs.

drawbacks.text: The caps apply only where the harm is purely financial, which is exactly where defendants tend to be large companies and plaintiffs tend to be individual consumers with little bargaining power — so the bill would narrow accountability most where consumers are least able to protect themselves otherwise [S2][S3].

If any party requests a split proceeding, evidence about the misconduct relevant only to punitive damages would be barred from the compensatory-damages phase, meaning the jury deciding the base award would not hear the worst of the conduct [S2].
The bill would override state court procedures nationwide for covered cases, applying federal limits even in states whose legislatures had chosen not to cap punitive damages [S2].

Supporters' strongest points: the bill carves out cases involving death, serious permanent injury, drunk or drugged driving, and convicted violent or sexual offenses, so the worst physical-harm cases are untouched, and it does not preempt stricter state limits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For businesses, the predictability is real: a firm facing a fraud or bad-faith suit would know its worst-case punitive exposure in advance, and honest small operators would get a lower cap still. But the cost falls on people who have already been financially wronged: the higher proof standard and the caps would let a company that knowingly cheats customers plan the penalty into the cost of doing business, and state laws offering stronger remedies would be overridden. Weighing it, the bill trades deterrence against financial misconduct for liability predictability, and the people who lose that deterrence are ordinary consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee in October 1998 and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, which kills a bill automatically.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Hyde introduced the bill on October 10, 1998, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1].
No further action appears in the record — no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action — before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].
The bill was introduced in the final weeks of a two-year Congress, late in an election year, when an unreported committee bill has almost no chance of reaching the floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plaintiffs and consumers came out better off, because state and federal courts kept existing punitive-damages rules, and companies facing lawsuits over financial misconduct kept full exposure under current law. Trial lawyers, whose fees depend on the size of awards, also benefited from the bill's death.

for.name: Henry Hyde
for.role: U.S. Representative (IL-6) and Chair, House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which he chaired.

for.name: James Moran
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the record shows a Republican lead sponsor with one Democratic cosponsor, a pattern typical of business-backed tort reform [S4].

industries.note: Punitive damages are a major remedy in bad-faith insurance cases, where an insurer refuses to pay a legitimate claim. Capping and restricting those awards would cut the industry's largest liability exposure in exactly the cases where the policyholder has already been wronged.

industries.industry: Large corporations facing financial-injury suits (banks, finance, product and service companies)
industries.note: Nearly half of punitive awards come in financial-injury cases, which are brought mostly against corporate defendants. The bill's cap and higher proof standard would make the worst-case cost of misconduct predictable and bounded.

Entities with fewer than 25 employees would get an even lower cap (the lesser of three times loss or $250,000), limiting what customers and counterparties could recover in punitive damages against them.

Contingency-fee lawyers' income scales with award size, so caps and a split trial procedure that hides misconduct evidence from the compensatory jury would reduce both recoveries for clients and fees for the bar. Their interest in this bill runs alongside injured consumers'.
